Let’s talk about something that quietly shapes almost everything we see, feel, and believe—language and storytelling.
Words have an incredible power. They set the boundaries for what we think is possible. Every story we hear, every joke we tell, every label we use—they’re all building the invisible walls around our world.
Ever notice how a single word can open a door, or just slam it shut? Think about the child who’s told again and again, “boys don’t cry” or “girls are too emotional.” These aren’t just passing comments. They sink in. They teach kids what’s okay to feel, what’s admired, and what’s off-limits. Fast forward a few years, and those kids—now adults—find themselves struggling to show emotion, or chasing dreams that don’t match the story they were handed.
And it’s not just family or friends. The stories we see in the media matter, too. When women are only shown as helpers or love interests, it sends a message—loud and clear—about what’s valued. When men are always the strong, silent heroes, it boxes them in. Most of us don’t even notice these patterns... until someone points them out. And once you see them, it’s almost impossible to ignore.
But here’s something powerful—language isn’t just a mirror. It’s also a tool for change. When people start naming injustice, calling out harassment, or challenging stereotypes, things begin to shift. Just sharing one honest story can make someone out there feel less alone. It can spark a conversation, or even light the fuse for a movement.
There’s real power in sharing your own experiences. When someone says, “This happened to me,” it invites empathy. Suddenly, it’s not just an abstract idea—it’s real. Others start to see themselves in the story, to recognize their own struggles, their own hopes. The more these stories are told, the harder it is for anyone to pretend that inequality is rare, or that it doesn’t matter.
Of course, language can also throw up barriers. Some words carry a lot of baggage. They can make people feel left out, or even attacked. Take the word “feminist”—sometimes, it’s misunderstood, thrown around like an insult or a threat. But claiming that word, and explaining what it really means—a belief in fairness, in dignity, in the right to choose your own path—takes real courage.
Changing how we talk? It’s not easy. Old habits have a way of sticking around, and there’s often pushback. But every time someone chooses a kinder word, tells a more honest story, or just listens with an open mind, something shifts. It might seem small, but over time, all these little changes add up. And that’s how we make room for new possibilities.
